turns.content: The emergency rule dropped yesterday afternoon. I need a triage workflow that keeps our terminals compliant but doesn't make patrons walk out the second they see a camera.

Happy to help build that out — but first I need to know which emergency rule we're dealing with, because "terminals + cameras + patrons" could mean a few different industries (skill-game/amusement terminals, video lottery, sweepstakes cafés, cannabis retail kiosks, etc.), and the compliance triage looks very different for each.

Quick questions:

1. **What jurisdiction and agency?** (e.g., state gaming commission, lottery board, liquor/cannabis control) — and do you have the rule text or a link?
2. **What does the rule actually mandate?** Continuous camera coverage of each terminal? Retention period? Signage/disclosure to patrons? Facial recognition or just recording?
3. **What's your footprint?** How many terminals, how many locations, and do you already have camera infrastructure or is this net-new install?
4. **What's the compliance deadline and penalty?** Immediate effect, grace period, or enforcement discretion?

Once I know that, I can draft a triage workflow that typically looks like:

- **Phase 1 (48–72 hrs):** Gap audit per location — map existing camera coverage vs. required sightlines, flag dead zones, inventory signage.
- **Phase 2:** Low-friction fixes first — reposition existing cameras, add dome cameras (less confrontational than visible bullet cams pointed at seats), post friendly disclosure signage framed as "for your security" rather than surveillance language.
- **Phase 3:** Patron-experience guardrails — no cameras at eye level facing patrons directly, staff talking points so floor staff can explain it in one sentence without sounding alarming, and a complaint-escalation path.
- **Ongoing:** Retention/storage compliance check, incident log, and a weekly spot-audit so you can show a good-faith compliance trail if inspectors show up.

Tell me the rule details and I'll turn this into a concrete, assignable checklist with owners and deadlines.
State rule, not gaming. Department of Consumer Protection, emergency public internet terminal rule. No cameras—identity-verification *software* before anyone can access restricted categories.

Got it — that reframes things. This is an age/ID-verification-gating problem at the software layer, not a surveillance problem, which is actually good news for patron experience: done right, the verification step can feel like a login screen, not a checkpoint. Here's a triage workflow built for that.

## Phase 1 — Rule interpretation & scoping (24–48 hrs)

- **Pin down the exact trigger language.** "Restricted categories" definitions matter enormously — does the rule define them by content type (adult, gambling-adjacent, etc.), by URL category lists, or by your filtering taxonomy? Get counsel or your compliance lead to write a one-page plain-English interpretation memo. Every downstream decision hangs on this.
- **Clarify verification standard:** Does the rule say *age* verification (18+/21+) or full *identity* verification? Document scan? Knowledge-based questions? Credit-header check? Liveness? The acceptable methods list determines your vendor shortlist.
- **Check the exemptions and edge cases:** staff-assisted access, terminals in employee-only areas, minors accompanied by adults, accessibility accommodations. These are where enforcement complaints actually come from.
- **Inventory your estate:** every public terminal, its OS, its current filtering/content-control stack, network segmentation, and whether it's managed centrally or per-location.

## Phase 2 — Technical triage (days 2–7)

- **Tier your terminals:**
  - *Tier A:* Terminals on managed, modern platforms → can take a software gate quickly.
  - *Tier B:* Older hardware/OS → may need a network-level gate (verification portal at the captive-portal layer) instead of endpoint software.
  - *Tier C:* Anything that can't support either → take offline or restrict to a whitelisted kiosk mode until remediated. Document why.
- **Pick your gating architecture.** For most public-terminal operators the least-friction option is: default-deny for restricted categories at the filter layer → patron hits a verification interstitial → passes → session-level unlock with a timeout. That avoids per-site re-verification, which is what makes patrons walk out.
- **Vendor evaluation on three axes:** verification speed (target under 60 seconds), data-handling posture (does PII stay with the vendor, is it deleted after verification — this matters under consumer-protection law), and false-rejection rate.

## Phase 3 — Patron experience guardrails (parallel, not after)

- **One verification per session, not per site.** Non-negotiable for retention.
- **Design the interstitial like a library card prompt, not a border crossing:** plain language ("State law requires a quick age check to access some sites"), no red warning styling, show expected time ("takes about 30 seconds").
- **Offer a low-friction path for patrons who won't or can't verify:** unrestricted categories still work instantly, and staff can hand out a printed "what you can still access" card. Most patrons never touch a restricted category — make sure their experience is *unchanged*.
- **Staff talking points:** one sentence, no judgment — "The state now requires a quick age check for certain websites; it takes about 30 seconds and we don't keep your info." Script the follow-up for frustrated patrons too.
- **Accessibility check:** screen-reader compatibility of the verification flow, alternatives for patrons without ID (if the rule permits any).

## Phase 4 — Compliance evidence & ongoing ops

- **Build the audit trail the DCP will ask for:** verification logs (timestamps, pass/fail, no unnecessary PII), software version records per terminal, takedown/offline documentation for Tier C machines, and staff training sign-offs.
- **Weekly spot-audit:** attempt restricted-category access without verification on a sample of terminals; log results.
- **Assign a single owner** for DCP correspondence and a deadline for written questions to the agency — emergency rules often get clarified or amended within weeks, and you want to be on record with good-faith compliance questions.
- **Watch for the permanent rulemaking:** emergency rules typically expire (often 90–180 days). Track the comment period; the final rule may soften or tighten verification methods.

Two things that would sharpen this: (1) which state's DCP issued it — I can flag known quirks of that agency's enforcement style — and (2) your rough terminal count and whether they're centrally managed, which determines whether Phase 2 is a weekend push or a month-long rollout. Okay, this is helpful. I need the talk track for the desk volunteers—how to explain the verification without scaring people. Draft that for me

Here's a desk-ready talk track — built to be skimmed mid-shift, so it's structured as a one-pager your volunteers can keep at the desk.

---

# Desk Volunteer Talk Track: The New Age-Verification Step

## The one-liner (use this 90% of the time)

> "The state now requires a quick age check before accessing certain websites. It takes about 30 seconds, and we don't see or keep your information."

Say it warmly and matter-of-factly, like mentioning the Wi-Fi password. Tone does more than wording here — if you treat it as routine, patrons will too.

## If someone asks follow-up questions

**"Why do I have to do this?"**
> "It's a new state rule for public computers, not something we decided ourselves. Every place with public terminals is doing it now."

**"What happens to my information?"**
> "The check is done by a secure verification service, and the library doesn't see or store your ID details. It just confirms yes-or-no, then lets you through."

**"Do I have to do it every time I visit a website?"**
> "No — once per session. After that, everything works like normal until you log off."

**"What if I don't want to verify?"**
> "Totally fine — most of the internet still works without it. Only certain restricted categories are behind the check. Everything else is exactly the same as before."

**"I don't have an ID with me."**
> "No problem — you can still use the terminal for everything outside the restricted categories. Here, I'll show you what's available." *(Then walk them through it or hand them the printed access card.)*

**"Is the government watching what I look at?"**
> "No. The system only checks that someone is old enough — it doesn't record or report what sites anyone visits."

## If a patron is frustrated

1. **Acknowledge first, explain second:** "I hear you — it is an extra step, and it caught all of us off guard too."
2. **Give them the fastest path forward:** "If you want, I can walk you through it right now — it's genuinely about 30 seconds."
3. **Offer the no-verify option without making it feel like a punishment:** "Or if you'd rather skip it, everything outside the restricted list works right away."
4. **If they want to complain beyond you:** "I can give you the contact for the state agency that issued the rule — they'll want to hear it directly." *(Have the DCP contact info printed at the desk. This redirects heat upward and out of your building.)*

## Things NOT to say

- ❌ "We have to verify your **identity**" — sounds like a background check. Say **"age check."**
- ❌ "It's to stop people from looking at **bad stuff**" — judgmental and vague. Say **"certain restricted categories."**
- ❌ "Your info is totally safe, don't worry" — overpromising invites suspicion. Use the calm, factual version: *"we don't see or keep it."*
- ❌ "It's because of the new emergency rule" — bureaucratic language raises alarm. **"New state rule"** is enough.
- ❌ Never speculate about *why* the state issued the rule, even if a patron pushes. "I just know it's a state requirement that applies to all public terminals" is the full answer.

## Golden rule for volunteers

**You are not enforcing anything — you're helping someone through a 30-second step.** If a patron becomes hostile or you feel unsafe, don't argue; hand it to a supervisor.

---

A few notes on how to deploy this:

- **Print it as a two-sided card** (one-liner + FAQs on one side, "don't say" list on the other) and laminate one per desk.
- **Pair it with the printed "what you can still access" card** mentioned in the workflow — volunteers need something to physically hand people, which defuses tension better than words alone.
- **Do a 15-minute run-through** before your next shift change: one person plays the frustrated patron, one plays the desk. The first time anyone says the one-liner out loud shouldn't be to an actual patron.
- If your patron base includes significant non-English speakers, tell me which languages and I'll translate the one-liner and top three FAQs.

Want me to also draft the interstitial screen text patrons see on the terminal itself, so the screen language and the volunteer language match? Mismatched wording between the two is a common trust-killer.
The laminated card is good. Now I need the script for the interstitial screen itself. Keep it warm and short

Here's the interstitial copy, screen by screen. It's written to match the volunteer talk track word-for-word where it counts ("quick age check," "about 30 seconds," "we don't see or keep your information") — that consistency is what makes patrons believe both.

---

## Screen 1 — The gate (what patrons see when they hit a restricted site)

> **Quick age check**
>
> A state rule requires a one-time age check to visit certain websites on public computers.
>
> It takes about 30 seconds, and we don't see or keep your information.
>
> [ **Continue** ]
>
> *Rather skip it? Everything else on the internet works without the check.* [Go back]

Notes: "Continue," not "Verify" or "Submit ID." The escape hatch is visible *before* the button — people who feel they have a choice almost always proceed.

## Screen 2 — While verification runs

> **Checking...**
>
> This usually takes a few seconds. Thanks for your patience.

If it runs long (10+ seconds), add a line:

> Still working — hang tight. If this takes more than a minute, flag down a staff member and we'll help.

## Screen 3 — Success

> **You're all set!**
>
> You won't be asked again during this session.
>
> [ **Continue to the site** ]

## Screen 4 — Verification didn't pass

> **We couldn't complete the age check.**
>
> This can happen for lots of ordinary reasons. You can try again, or a staff member at the desk can help — no judgment, we promise.
>
> [ **Try again** ]  [ **Go back** ]

Note: "couldn't complete," never "failed" or "denied." Most rejections are lighting, camera angle, or typos — the copy should assume that.

## Screen 5 — Patron declines / no ID

> **No problem.**
>
> You can keep browsing — only certain restricted categories need the check. Everything else works as usual.
>
> [ **Back to browsing** ]

---

Deployment notes:

- **Reading level:** This is written around a 6th-grade level; keep it there. Short sentences are doing the trust-building.
- **Button hierarchy:** One primary button per screen, always the forward path. Secondary options in lighter styling.
- **The "about 30 seconds" promise:** Time your actual vendor flow before launch. If it averages 90 seconds, change the copy to "about a minute" — a broken time promise on screen 1 poisons everything after it.
- **Match the card:** The phrase *"we don't see or keep your information"* now appears in the talk track, on screen 1, and should also appear in your printed FAQ. One claim, repeated identically, everywhere.
- **Translation:** If you told me your top non-English patron languages, I'd localize screens 1, 4, and 5 first — those are the three moments where confusion turns into a walkout.

Want me to also draft the tiny footer line for the terminal's home page ("Some sites require a quick age check — state rule, takes 30 seconds")? A heads-up *before* patrons hit the wall cuts the surprise factor roughly in half.
The home screen footer is exactly what I need. Draft that too, matching the same warm tone

Here's the footer copy, with a few length options since "footer" can mean anything from a full banner strip to a single line squeezed under your navigation:

---

## Option A — Standard footer line (recommended default)

> **Heads up:** Some websites require a quick age check — it's a state rule, takes about 30 seconds, and we don't see or keep your information.

This is the one I'd ship. One sentence, three reassurances, same vocabulary as the card and the interstitial.

## Option B — Short version (for tight layouts)

> Some sites need a quick age check (state rule) — about 30 seconds, no info kept.

## Option C — Two-part version (if your footer has a link)

> **New state rule:** a quick age check is required for some websites. [Learn more →]

The "Learn more" link should open a small pop-up with three lines:

> **What it is:** A one-time age check before certain websites — it takes about 30 seconds.
> **Your privacy:** The check is handled by a secure service. We don't see or keep your information.
> **Your choice:** Skip it anytime — everything outside the restricted categories works as usual.

---

Deployment notes:

- **Keep "Heads up" or drop it based on your house style.** It adds warmth, but if your home screen already uses casual language elsewhere, it blends; if the rest of your site is formal, it may stand out oddly — in that case start with "Please note:" which is formal but still soft.
- **Don't make it red or use a warning icon.** Neutral or your brand color, same font size as other footer text. The goal is that patrons absorb it passively — an alarm-styled footer creates the very anxiety it's trying to prevent.
- **Consistency check across your full set now:** the phrase *"quick age check"* appears on the volunteer card, interstitial screen 1, and this footer. *"About 30 seconds"* and *"we don't see or keep your information"* appear in all three as well. Patrons who hear it from a volunteer, then read it on the home screen, then see it on the gate experience it as one coherent message — that's the trust mechanism.
- **One deliberate omission:** no mention of "restricted categories" in the footer. "Some websites" is enough at this stage; the specifics only matter at the moment someone actually hits the gate.

If you tell me the pixel width or character limit of your footer area, I can trim Option A to fit exactly. And if your home screen has a staff-notices or announcements section, I can draft a slightly longer version for that spot too — though I'd keep the footer as the short one.
